ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: From the front view, the maximum heights of the 4 front-facing columns in order are [3,4,3,3], that is, the second column is highest at 4, and the other three columns are 3. From the right-side view, the maximum heights of the 4 depth rows in order are [4,3,2,3]. From the top view, it is a 4×4 grid, and the positions where there are actually blocks are 1110 / 1101 / 1011 / 0111, for a total of 12 positions where vertical stacks can be placed. Reasoning: Let the front heights be F=[3,4,3,3], and the right-side heights be R=[4,3,2,3]. John uses as many blocks as possible, so every cell that has a position in the top view is filled to the maximum height allowed by the restrictions in the two directions, namely height min(F column, R row). Compute the maximum number of blocks by row: row 1 1110, corresponding height 3+4+3=10; row 2 1101, corresponding height 3+3+3=9; row 3 1011, corresponding height 2+2+2=6; row 4 0111, corresponding height 3+3+3=9. Therefore John originally used at most 10+9+6+9=34 blocks. Now find the minimum number of blocks that keeps the three views unchanged. The 12 positions in the top view must all retain at least 1 block, so first there are 12. Height 4 can only be realized at the intersection of front column 2 and right-side row 1, so that position must have height 4, which is 3 more than the base 1. The remaining front columns 1, 3, and 4 all need some place to reach height 3, so at least 3 stacks of height 3 are needed; for example, one can choose row 2 column 1, row 4 column 3, and row 2 column 4, which also covers the rows whose right-side height is 3, adding a total of 3×2=6 more than the base. Right-side row 3 has maximum height 2, so it still needs one stack of height 2, which is 1 more than the base. Thus the minimum number of blocks that keeps the three views is 12+3+6+1=22. At most 34-22=12 blocks can be removed.

method.method_draft: Use a height-table optimization. First read the views from the images: the front view has 4 columns with maximum heights [3,4,3,3]; the right-side view has 4 depth rows with maximum heights [4,3,2,3]; the top view is a 4 by 4 footprint with occupied pattern 1110 / 1101 / 1011 / 0111, i.e. 12 possible stack positions. From the text, John used as many cubes as possible, so at every occupied top-view cell put the tallest stack allowed by both relevant side projections: height = min(front-column height, right-row height). Summing these 12 stack heights gives the maximal original cube count. Then find the smallest cube count that still preserves the same three views: every occupied top-view cell must retain at least one cube, and for each front column and right-side row at least one retained stack must reach the required maximum height. Choose the forced height-4 stack at the intersection of front column 2 and right row 1; choose height-3 stacks to cover the remaining front columns and the right rows of height 3; add one height-2 stack in the right row whose maximum is 2. This gives the minimum preserved-view construction. Subtract minimum count from John’s maximum count to get the number removable, 12.

method.method_draft: Use a layer-by-layer projection-cover method. First describe the image data: the top view gives 12 occupied cells in a 4 by 4 footprint; the front view has all 4 columns present through height 3 and only the second column reaches height 4; the right view has all 4 rows present through height 2, rows 1, 2, and 4 reach height 3, and only row 1 reaches height 4. For John’s maximal construction, count cubes by horizontal layers: layer 1 has all 12 footprint cells, layer 2 also has all 12 cells, layer 3 has only footprint cells whose front column and right row both allow height at least 3, giving 9 cells, and layer 4 has only the intersection of front column 2 and right row 1, giving 1 cell. Thus the maximal count is 12+12+9+1. For Ana’s minimal remaining construction, layer 1 must still contain all 12 footprint cells to preserve the top view. Above that, count the minimum cells needed to make each projection still visible: layer 4 needs the single cell at column 2,row 1; layer 3 must cover all four front columns and the three right rows that reach height 3, requiring 4 cells; layer 2 must also cover the right row whose maximum is only 2, so it needs one additional cell beyond the layer-3 cells, for 5 cells total at layer 2. The minimum remaining count is 12+5+4+1, and the difference from the maximal layered count is 12.

Ana 要保留三个视图不变并尽量少留下方块。为了保持俯视图，第 1 层必须保留全部 12 个格子。第 4 层必须保留正面第 2 列与侧面第 1 行交点的 1 个方块。第 3 层需要让正面 4 列都仍能看到高度 3，同时让侧面第 1、2、4 行仍能看到高度 3，最少可用 4 个方块完成。第 2 层必须支撑这些第 3 层方块，并且还要让侧面第 3 行达到高度 2，所以在这 4 个方块之外还需要 1 个第 2 层方块，共 5 个。最少保留方块数为 12+5+4+1=22。

因此最多可移除 34-22=12 个方块。

raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: From the front view, the maximum heights of the 4 front-facing columns in order are [3,4,3,3], that is, the second column is highest at 4, and the other three columns are 3. From the right-side view, the maximum heights of the 4 depth rows in order are [4,3,2,3]. From the top view, it is a 4×4 grid, and the positions where there are actually blocks are 1110 / 1101 / 1011 / 0111, for a total of 12 positions where vertical stacks can be placed.

Reasoning: Let the front heights be F=[3,4,3,3], and the right-side heights be R=[4,3,2,3]. John uses as many blocks as possible, so every cell that has a position in the top view is filled to the maximum height allowed by the restrictions in the two directions, namely height min(F column, R row). Compute the maximum number of blocks by row: row 1 1110, corresponding height 3+4+3=10; row 2 1101, corresponding height 3+3+3=9; row 3 1011, corresponding height 2+2+2=6; row 4 0111, corresponding height 3+3+3=9. Therefore John originally used at most 10+9+6+9=34 blocks.

Now find the minimum number of blocks that keeps the three views unchanged. The 12 positions in the top view must all retain at least 1 block, so first there are 12. Height 4 can only be realized at the intersection of front column 2 and right-side row 1, so that position must have height 4, which is 3 more than the base 1. The remaining front columns 1, 3, and 4 all need some place to reach height 3, so at least 3 stacks of height 3 are needed; for example, one can choose row 2 column 1, row 4 column 3, and row 2 column 4, which also covers the rows whose right-side height is 3, adding a total of 3×2=6 more than the base. Right-side row 3 has maximum height 2, so it still needs one stack of height 2, which is 1 more than the base. Thus the minimum number of blocks that keeps the three views is 12+3+6+1=22. At most 34-22=12 blocks can be removed.
